title: DNA Analysis (Awareness Level)
desc: Understand what DNA tests can and cannot tell you, how samples are handled, and how to protect privacy and dignity. Awareness only.
outcomes: Explain DNA, genes and the main kinds of tests in plain words.
Read a sample report and say what it does and does not mean.
Weigh benefits and risks of sharing genetic data.
task: Produce a two-page plain-language explainer on DNA testing with a risk list and a consent checklist.
condition: A computer, public information, two peers and a mentor. You will not handle real samples or interpret anyone's results.
standard: Facts are correct and sourced; limits are stated; no diagnosis is offered; privacy risks are named; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Lab assistants, health communicators, teachers, curious adults.
modules: DNA in simple words
Understand
DNA is the instruction code in cells.
Genes are sections of DNA; we inherit them from parents.
Most traits come from many genes and the environment.
A test reads some parts, not everything.
Height depends on many genes and on food and health in childhood.
Draw a simple DNA to trait picture.
Picture has no false claims.
Kinds of tests
Understand
Tests differ in purpose.
Ancestry, health risk, carrier, paternity, forensic.
A test result is a probability, not destiny.
Medical tests belong with a clinician.
A carrier test shows chance of passing on a condition, not that a child will have it.
Compare three test types in a table.
Table states purpose and limit.
From sample to result
Analyse
Many steps can go wrong.
Collect, label, store, extract, read, report.
Chain of custody records who held the sample.
Contamination and labelling errors cause false results.
A mislabelled tube swaps two results; a barcode check prevents it.
Map the steps and risks.
Every step has a quality check.
Reading a result
Analyse
Results need context.
Percent and risk numbers explain chance, not certainty.
Variants of uncertain meaning are common.
Only a genetic counsellor or clinician explains health results.
A report says a 1.5 times higher chance; absolute risk goes from 2 to 3 in 100.
Explain a sample number to a peer.
Peer repeats it correctly.
Marketing and overclaims
Evaluate
Be careful with big promises.
Beware "find your perfect diet by DNA" or "know your talent".
Look for evidence, regulation and independent reviews.
Price does not prove quality.
An ad claims a diet plan from DNA; no study is shown. The learner marks it as unproven.
Review two adverts.
Overclaims named with reasons.
Privacy and family impact
Evaluate
Your DNA reveals things about relatives.
Data may be sold, hacked or used by insurers in some places.
Findings can surprise families, such as unknown relatives.
Consent must be informed and free.
A family agrees before testing that no one will be told surprises without a counsellor.
Write a consent checklist.
Eight clear questions.
Ethics and fairness
Evaluate
Genetic data must not be used to discriminate.
No test should be forced by employers or schools.
Respect culture and faith views.
Data from some groups is underrepresented, so results can be less accurate.
A study notes fewer data from certain populations and urges wider sampling.
Discuss two cases with peers.
Peers reach a reasoned view.
Write the explainer
Create
Combine all parts.
Use short sentences.
Add a glossary and a where-to-get-help box.
Test with a non-expert.
A reader says, "Now I know to ask a counsellor, not a website."
Finish and test.
Reader can state three limits of DNA tests.
quiz: Ancestry and carrier (or health risk, paternity).
To show who held the sample.
A big promise with no evidence.
Sale, hacking or misuse by insurers.
Results are less accurate for under-represented groups.
rubric: Clear and tested with a reader
Every claim linked to a dated record and checked by a peer
Checked, dated and explained to others

L2: learner can name the test kinds.

L4: learner can check a sample chain.
L5: learner can review ads and consent.
L6: learner can coordinate consent records.
L7: learner can audit an explainer.
